First-, second- and third-party
Your guide places synthetic fraud in first-party, intentional money muling in second-party, and ATO/unintentional mulling in third-party. Classify by who is involved, then identify the mechanism.
APP fraud vs. ATO
APP: the deceived victim authorizes the payment. ATO: a criminal gains unauthorized control of an existing account.
Precision vs. recall
Precision = TP/(TP+FP): how many flagged cases were genuine fraud? Recall = TP/(TP+FN): how much genuine fraud was caught?
Supervised vs. unsupervised
Supervised learning trains on labeled cases. Unsupervised methods find patterns without requiring known fraud labels.
Inherent vs. residual risk
Inherent risk is exposure before controls; residual risk is exposure remaining after controls.
Alert vs. concluded fraud
An alert initiates triage; documented, sufficient evidence supports conclusions, action and closure.
US Regulation E vs. UK payment regimes
Do not confuse US unauthorized EFT investigation deadlines with UK unauthorized payment refunds or APP scam reimbursement arrangements.
Evidence vs. red flags
An indicator guides further inquiry. Evidence must be relevant, authenticated and handled with integrity to support an investigation finding.
Fraud mitigation life cycle
Think of controls across onboarding, active relationship, detection, response and customer exit, followed by a feedback loop.
Rules vs. analytics models
Rules apply explicit conditions and thresholds; models can find richer patterns. Choose tools based on evidence, customer impact and data quality.
CNP vs. counterfeit card
Card-not-present uses details in remote transactions; counterfeit card fraud involves a cloned physical card at point of sale.
Root cause vs. typology
Typology explains how the scheme worked; root-cause analysis explains what organizational weakness allowed it to occur or persist.
